title: Ang 40–42: Guru Ram Das
hookLine: the fourth Guru's short run of hymns
tomorrow: when a day hits you like a blast of heat, where do you stand?
last: THE EVENING PAGES · THE GATEWAY · THE FIRST RAGA.

lines: ANG 40: AT THE SIDE OF THE ROAD.
cards: A map app will reroute you a dozen times without complaint. But some choices come with no map at all: stay or go, this job or that one, say yes or wait.
On ang forty, a Guru describes standing in exactly that spot, at the side of a road, not knowing the way. And he doesn't pretend otherwise.

teach.h: SRI RAG, MAHALA 4: GURU RAM DAS.
teach.b: The heading reads Sri Rag, Mahala 4: Guru Ram Das, the same voice as the So Purakh hymns of the evening. His run in Sri Rag is short, a few pages, and it's full of longing.

teach.h: I STAND BY THE ROAD, ASKING.
teach.b: In paraphrase, one hymn says: I stand by the road every day, asking the way. If anyone would show me my Beloved, I would go with them.

teach.h: FOLLOW THOSE WHO KNOW THE WAY.
teach.b: Those who have met my Beloved, I would follow behind them. Something to tell someone tonight: in the Granth, asking for directions isn't a weakness. It's the whole posture of the hymn.
The speaker doesn't fake a map. There's no shame in the line, only honesty, and a little hope. He stands where the road is, asks, and follows the people who've been where he wants to go.
That's the fourth Guru's short run: a few pages of wanting, and the courage to ask.

how: Guru Ram Das's hymns in Sri Rag stand on angs 40 to 42, between Guru Amar Das's hymns and Guru Arjan's; Sikhs read them in order in a sehaj path, and sing them in kirtan.

s: Guru Ram Das's Sri Rag hymns fill dozens of pages
his run here is short, angs 40 to 42; then the fifth Guru's hymns begin.
in the hymn, the speaker stands by the road asking the way
and would follow anyone who has met the Beloved.
the hymn treats asking the way as a weakness
asking is the hymn's whole posture: ask, and follow those who know the way.

games.q: a new kid is lost in the hallways on the first day but won't ask anyone, because it would look bad. what does Guru Ram Das's hymn offer?
o: wait it out; asking only proves you're lost.
ask someone who knows the way, and follow them.
skip the day and try again when it's less crowded.
games.why: the speaker stands by the road every day, asking the way, and would follow those who've met the Beloved. asking isn't the weakness; it's the way in.

practice: If you can, stand and walk slowly for a minute, across a room or down a hallway, as if along a road. With each step, let one question you're carrying come along, without needing an answer.
Then sit, and think of one person who knows a way you're looking for.
